title: Balance on one leg: a quiet test of steady
description: Standing on one leg looks like nothing. Done slowly, beside a wall, it trains the ankles, hips and inner ear that keep you upright — and it quietly measures how steady you are.

body.heading: Set up safely
paragraphs: Stand side-on to a wall or a sturdy chair, close enough to touch. Lift one foot just off the floor and time yourself. Most of the work happens invisibly: your ankle makes dozens of tiny corrections a minute, and your eyes and inner ear feed it constant reports.
Swap legs — almost everyone has a steadier side. Note both times; the gap between them is as interesting as the numbers themselves.

body.heading: Make it a practice, not a contest
paragraphs: A few short stands a day, perhaps while the kettle boils, genuinely improve balance over weeks, because the correction system learns like any other skill. Progress means longer, calmer stands — not heroic ones.
Stop the moment you need to hop or grab hard, and never practise where a fall would land on something sharp or hard. Steady is built slowly, which is rather the point.

takeaway: Practise short one-leg stands beside a wall, both sides, a few times a day: balance improves quietly, and steady is built slowly.
materials: A wall or sturdy chair to stand beside
supervision: An adult should stay beside younger children and anyone unsteady; this is a supported exercise, not a dare.
safetyNotes: Always practise within reach of the wall or chair.
Stop at once if you feel dizzy.
Never practise on wet, sloped or cluttered floors.
